Assignment 2 – Case Study Lab

Stage 2 Lab Activities

SmartCare Requirements Engineering

AI OFF -> AI ON -> VERIFY | 1 hour

# Learning objectives

- Analyze the SmartCare client brief.
- Identify stakeholders and scope.
- Write functional and non-functional requirements.
- Develop user stories and Given-When-Then acceptance criteria.
- Use AI to critique requirements without allowing it to invent stakeholder needs.
- Produce SmartCare Requirements Specification v1.0.

# Part A - Client Brief: AI OFF

SmartCare uses spreadsheets and paper records. Staff report duplicate bookings, difficulty finding patient information, inconsistent appointment status and limited appointment history. Management wants a small, maintainable patient, practitioner and appointment system.

# Part B - Stakeholders and Scope: AI OFF

Identify at least four stakeholders. Create In Scope and Out of Scope lists. Label uncertain features as provisional rather than confirmed.

| **Stakeholder**               | **Role**                                  | **Primary Need**                                                                                                   |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| _Clinic Receptionist_         | Day-to-day appointment booking operations | Quick patient lookup, easy appointment scheduling, cancellation management, status updates                         |
| _General Practitioners (GPs)_ | Clinical staff providing consultations    | View their schedule, see confirmed appointments, access patient medical history, manage availability               |
| _Clinic Manager_              | Administrative oversight and reporting    | Create operational reports, track appointment statistics, assess practitioner effort, and detect booking patterns. |
| _Patients_                    | Healthcare consumers                      | View/book appointments, receive confirmations, manage cancellations, access appointment history                    |

\- In scope:

- Patient registration and profile management
- Book and schedule appointments.
- Calendar of available practitioners
- Appointment Status Tracking (pending, confirmed, completed, canceled)
- Basic appointment history
- Appointment cancelation and rescheduling
- Operational reporting (appointment counts, utilization rates).

\- Out of scope (Provisional / Uncertain):

- Clinical patient health records.
- Insurance and billing integration
- SMS/email notification system.
- Online patient self-service portal.
- Multiple-location support
- Integration of external healthcare systems

# Part C - Functional Requirements: AI OFF

Write 8-12 numbered functional requirements using FR-01, FR-02 and so on. Each should describe one observable capability.

FR-01: Patient registration 🡺 The system must allow receptionists to build new patient profiles including the patient's name, contact information (phone, email), date of birth, and medical history notes.

FR-02: Patient Search and Retrieval 🡺 The system should allow receptionists to rapidly search for current patients by name or patient ID in order to avoid creating duplicate patient records.

FR-03: Appointment booking 🡺 The system will allow receptionists to arrange appointments by selecting a patient, practitioner, and available time window.

FR-04: Duplicate booking prevention 🡺 The system must restrict the same practitioner from reserving several time slots on the same day.

FR-05: Appointment Status Management 🡺 The system must support appointment status transitions: Pending → Confirmed → Completed or Cancelled.

FR-06: Practitioner Availability Calendar. The system must provide practitioner availability (working hours, planned appointments, and blocked time) to allow receptionists to find available slots.

FR-07: Appointment Cancelation. The system allows receptionists to cancel appointments while saving the cause and timestamp.

FR-08: Appointment Rescheduling The system allows receptionists to reschedule an existing appointment without producing duplicates.

FR-9: Appointment History 🡺 The system must keep a complete record of all appointments (scheduled, completed, and canceled) with timestamps for audit trail purposes.

FR-10: Operational Reporting 🡺 The system generates information on total appointments, practitioner usage rates, cancelation rates, and booking trends by time and day.

FR-11: Data Validation 🡺 The system must check all user inputs (patient names, dates, and times) and provide unambiguous error messages when invalid data is entered.

FR 12: Role-Based Access Control 🡺 The system will restrict access based on the user's role: receptionist (booking/cancellation), practitioner (view schedule), and manager (view reports).

# Part D - Non-Functional Requirements: AI OFF

Write 4-6 numbered non-functional requirements covering appropriate qualities such as reliability, maintainability, usability, data integrity or testability.

NFR-01: Reliability 🡺 The system must maintain 99% uptime during clinic operation hours (7 AM - 5 PM, Monday through Friday) and prevent data loss in the event of an unexpected shutdown.

NFR-02: Usability 🡺 The system interface must be simple enough for clinic staff with limited computer experience to arrange appointments in less than 2 minutes without help.

NFR-03: Data Integrity 🡺 The system will use locking mechanisms to prevent concurrent booking conflicts and ensure appointment data consistency across all operations.

NFR-04: Maintainability 🡺 The system code must be well-documented and modular so that clinic IT personnel can add new features or resolve faults without rewriting core functionality.

NFR-05: Performance 🡺 The system must react to appointment searches in 2 seconds and appointment bookings in 3 seconds, regardless of database size.

NFR-06: Security 🡺 The system must require user authentication for all staff access and encrypt private patient information (phone number, email address, date of birth).

# Part E - User Stories and Acceptance Criteria: AI OFF

Write 4-6 user stories. For at least 3, create Given-When-Then acceptance criteria including failure scenario.

\- User Story 1: The receptionist books an appointment.

As a receptionist, I wish to plan appointments for patients to avoid disputes with paper records.

\*Acceptance criteria:\*

1. Given that a patient exists in the system. When I searched for the patient 🡺 The system then displays matching results with patient names and IDs.
2. Given that I have selected a patient. When I choose a practitioner 🡺 The system then displays all available time slots for that practitioner for the next four weeks.
3. Given that I have chosen a time slot. When I confirm the booking. The appointment shows in the practitioner's calendar, and a confirmation message is displayed.
4. Given that a practitioner is already booked at that time. When I try to book the same time. The system then displays an error notice saying "This time slot is unavailable" and does not set the appointment.

\- User Story 2: Receptionist Terminates an Appointment.

As a receptionist, I wish to cancel appointments to save up time for patients who need to reschedule.

\*Acceptance criteria:\*

1. Given I am viewing a confirmed appointment. When I click the cancel button 🡺 Then, the system prompts me to submit a cancelation reason.
2. Given I've entered a cancelation reason. When I confirm the cancelation 🡺 The appointment status switches to "Cancelled" and the time slot becomes available for future bookings.
3. Given that an appointment is canceled When I check the appointment history 🡺 The cancelation reason and timestamp are permanently preserved.
4. Given an appointment was canceled. When I try to cancel it again 🡺 The system then displays an error message: "This appointment is already canceled" and does not allow duplicate cancelation.

\- User Story 3: Practitioner looks over Schedule.

As a general practitioner, I should see my daily appointment schedule to prepare for forthcoming consultations.

\*Acceptance criteria:\*

1. Given I'm logged in as a practitioner When I access the schedule section 🡺 Then I see today's appointments in chronological sequence, with the patient names and appointment times.
2. Given I'm viewing my schedule When hovering over an appointment 🡺 The system then displays patient contact information and appointment notes.
3. Given there are no appointments booked. When I review my schedule 🡺 The system then displays "No appointments scheduled for today".

\- User Story 4: Clinic Manager Views Appointment Statistics.

🡺 As a clinic manager, I want to analyze appointment data and reports to track operational efficiency.

# Part F - AI Requirements Review: AI ON

Prompt: Act as a software requirements reviewer. Review the SmartCare requirements for ambiguity, inconsistency, missing clarification questions and testability. Do NOT invent new client requirements. For every suggestion, state whether it is based on evidence or is only a question/assumption requiring validation.

# Part G - VERIFY the AI Review

Classify each significant AI suggestion as Accepted, Modified, Rejected, or Unverified. Explain the evidence used.

| **AI Suggestion**                                                               | **Classification**  | **Evidence**                                                                                                                                                                      | **Verification**                                                                                                                                                                                                           | **Status** |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- |
| _Standardize modal verbs to "must"_                                             | ACCEPTED            | Direct comparison shows FR-02 uses "should" while FR-01,04-07,09,11 use "must" - inconsistent language weakens testability                                                        | Re-checked all FRs: confirmed mixed verbs exist. Standardizing to "must" aligns with IEEE 830 requirements standards                                                                                                       | ✓ VERIFIED |
| _FR-04 clarify overlapping vs. single appointment_                              | ACCEPTED & MODIFIED | Original text ambiguous: "prevent booking same practitioner...same day" could mean max 1 appt/day (contradicts clinic ops where practitioners see 5-10 patients/day)              | Clinic domain knowledge confirms: practitioners must handle multiple daily appointments. Revised language specifies "overlapping time slots" not "per day" limit. New requirement aligns with real-world clinic scheduling | ✓ VERIFIED |
| _NFR-04 add specific performance bounds_                                        | ACCEPTED            | Original: "regardless of database size" is unbounded and untestable. Contradicts "tested with 10,000 appointments"                                                                | Performance requirements need testable limits. Revised to "50,000 appointments, 5,000 patients" is measurable and traceable to typical clinic scale. Testable with load testing                                            | ✓ VERIFIED |
| _NFR-02/05 replace subjective with measurable metrics_                          | ACCEPTED            | "Minimal training" and "well-documented" lack objective criteria. Unmeasurable = untestable                                                                                       | Revised NFR-02: "<30 min training, <2 min booking" - objectively testable with stopwatch. Revised NFR-05: "PEP 8, docstrings, 80% coverage" - verifiable with tools (pylint, coverage.py)                                  | ✓ VERIFIED |
| _NFR-06 expand security: add in-transit encryption, key management, compliance_ | ACCEPTED & MODIFIED | Original only specifies "at rest" encryption; missing in-transit (TLS), key vault, and compliance framework. Security gap: unencrypted network traffic vulnerable to interception | Revised includes: AES-256 at rest + TLS 1.3 in transit + key vault storage + GDPR Article 32 compliance. Now comprehensive and verifiable through security audit                                                           | ✓ VERIFIED |

# Part H - Finalise SmartCare v0.2

Submit stakeholder analysis, scope, 8-12 FRs, 4-6 NFRs, 4-6 user stories, acceptance criteria, assumptions/open questions and selected AI review evidence.

# Reflection

In 150-250 words: What did AI notice that you missed? What did AI invent or overreach on? Which requirement changed after review? Why must requirements have evidence?

\- AI identified critical inconsistencies and gaps that human authors frequently overlook: the mixed modal verbs (must/should/will) that appeared minor but weakened testability across requirements; the logical ambiguity in FR-04 where "prevent booking same practitioner per day" could literally mean only one appointment allowed instead of preventing overlaps; and the mathematically untestable claim in NFR-04 that response times would remain constant "regardless of database size" despite subjective terminology such as "minimal training" and "well-documented" sound logical until you try to design an objective test for them, as does the insufficient security specification that covered encryption at rest but left network traffic unsecured.

\- Requirements must be traceable to stakeholder needs because without evidence, you can't justify why a feature exists, what it solves, or whether it's in scope; this traceability prevents scope creep and allows for accountability. This transition from subjective language to objective, verifiable criteria allow requirements to be checked using tools and stopwatches rather than opinions, decreasing ambiguity and enabling actual quality assurance.
